settings.description: Language used when a request specifies none. A request may always override it with ?lang= or an Accept-Language header.
Requests per minute allowed for one API key. Abuse protection, not billing.
Largest value a caller may pass to ?wait=. It bounds how long one request can hold a connection open.
How long one MCP tool call may run before it is cancelled.

Endpoints this instance serves without an API key, each written as '<METHOD> <path>' exactly as the API document shows it, for example 'GET /api/v1/unknown/video'. Empty means everything needs a credential, which is the default. Admin, authentication and setup endpoints can never be opened, whatever is listed here.

Keep parsed posts and authors in the database after the task result expires. With this off the instance keeps only its logs and metric history, and a post you parsed today cannot be looked up tomorrow.

How old a post's last existence check may be before it is checked again. This is what makes "which of the things I saved are gone" answerable at all - without it, a post deleted the day after it was archived stays marked live forever. 0 turns rechecking off.
How many posts one recheck pass verifies. Each is a real request through the identity pool, so this is the knob that decides what the answer costs.

Seconds between the individual requests a recheck or backfill makes. The scheduler paces requests per identity, which does nothing about a platform limit that counts requests per address - measured: 20 requests in 13 seconds were all rejected, while one a minute later succeeded. Nobody is waiting on these passes, so slow costs nothing.

Also keep each platform's untouched payload alongside the normalized record, so a new field can be back-computed later without re-crawling. Off by default: the parsers produce one for every object, making it the largest single thing this instance can choose to store.
How long a parsed user profile stays reusable.
How long a parsed video detail stays reusable before it is fetched again.
How long a parsed list page stays reusable. Lists change more often than a single item, so this is usually the shortest of the three.

Disk usage percent at which background collection and new download jobs stand down. Interactive API reads are never paused, and nothing is ever deleted - a full disk should degrade the instance, not take it offline or destroy what it has collected.
Disk usage percent at which this instance raises a warning. Measured on the filesystem, so it accounts for WAL, indexes and anything else sharing the volume.
Allow media downloads. Turning it off refuses new jobs and leaves stored files alone; nothing is deleted by this switch.

How much disk stored media may occupy. Past it the oldest unpinned downloads are removed until the volume is back under, and an alert says what went. Pinned downloads are never removed. 0 disables cleanup entirely.
Ceiling for one file, counted on bytes actually written rather than on the size the server claims. A transfer that reaches it is refused and leaves nothing behind.
How old an archived media link may be before a download re-parses the post to get fresh ones. Signed CDN links expire within hours; 0 always re-parses, which costs one request from the identity pool.
Where alerts are delivered: a list of channel descriptors, each with a type, a url and a language.
Master switch for outgoing alerts. Off means alerts are still recorded but nothing is sent.
Language for alert text, for channels that do not specify their own.
Assumed success rate for an identity with no history yet, between 0 and 1. It decides how eagerly a freshly minted identity is scheduled.
Low-water mark per platform. Dropping below it raises an alert and triggers minting.
How many identities the pool tries to keep per platform.

Delete archived posts last seen more than this many days ago. 0 means never delete, which is the default - the archive exists precisely to outlive the platform. Disk is protected by the capacity guard instead.
How long identity state changes are kept. Long enough to explain why an identity was retired.
How long per-request log rows are kept before they are dropped. Content snapshots are never deleted automatically.

How long a retired identity's row is kept after it is retired. The cookies are already wiped at retirement; this is only the record of the identity having existed, and without a window the table grows by one row for every identity the pool ever loses.
How long finished task rows are kept.
How long a task's result payload is kept. Shorter than the task row itself, because the payload is the bulky part.
How many distinct identities must be failing before an endpoint trips. This separates a broken endpoint from a single broken identity.
Minimum requests observed before an endpoint may trip, so a short burst of failures cannot open the circuit.
Risk-control rate above which an endpoint is tripped, between 0 and 1.
How long an identity rests after its first risk-control hit. Each consecutive hit doubles it.
Cooldown ceiling. An identity that reaches it is marked degraded instead of cooling again.
How long a request waits for a free identity before it degrades into a background task.
Maximum requests allowed to queue for an identity. Beyond this the API rejects immediately with Retry-After.
Whether cross-origin requests may carry cookies. Only meaningful with an explicit origin list; it cannot be combined with '*'.
Browser origins allowed to call this API. Empty means same-origin only. '*' would hand your API keys to any site the user visits.
Whether a task may call back to a caller-supplied URL. That URL is an SSRF vector, so this is off by default.

Whether a caller may pass ?proxy= to route their request through their own egress. 'deny' refuses the parameter, 'public' allows only publicly routable addresses, and 'any' also allows loopback and private ranges - which lets anyone holding an API key reach this server's own network.

Extra hostnames a short link may redirect through. The built-in platform list always applies; each entry is matched as a whole hostname, belongs to no platform, and widens the SSRF surface, so add one only to rescue a redirect chain that dies on an unlisted hop.

Shared secret used to sign task callbacks, sent as X-Dtk-Signature: sha256=<hmac of the exact body>. Without it a receiver has no way to tell a real notification from anyone who guessed the callback URL. Leave empty to send callbacks unsigned.
Whether the signer this mode does not prefer may still be used when the preferred one is unavailable. Turning it off is how you find out which signer is actually carrying the traffic.
Which signer produces the request signature: the browser, the in-process algorithms, or automatic switching between them.
Ceiling for a single browser-rpc signing call.
Deduplication window for the content history. A second snapshot of the same item inside this window is skipped rather than stored.
Whether this instance may contact the project to check for a newer release. It makes an outbound request, so it is opt-in.
How many due entries one tick may queue. The rest stay due and go on the next tick, so a large watchlist is spread over minutes rather than landing all at once in front of whoever is using the API.
Interval a newly watched target gets when none is specified.
Run scheduled collection. Turning it off leaves the entries and everything they have collected alone; it simply stops submitting runs.

Shortest interval any watched target may be given. A target collected every few seconds does not produce a better time series - it spends the whole identity pool on one author and starves everything else.
